Dear Secretary Reese:

Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) letter issued on
August 19, 2026,1 Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”) submits additional information2
concerning SPP’s proposed revisions filed in this proceeding.3

SPP respectfully requests that the Commission issue an order in this proceeding as soon as
practicable, but not later than November 18, 2026. This will allow SPP and its stakeholders
to have certainty regarding the implementation timeline for the provisions proposed in this
proceeding.

On April 17, 2026, SPP submitted revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff4 to (1)

On June 15, 2026, SPP filed an answer in response to comments and protests.16 The
MMU17 and the SPP TO Group18 filed answers in response to the SPP Answer.

In the August Letter, the Commission directed SPP to provide additional information
required to process the filing. The Commission required responses be submitted within
thirty (30) days of the date of the request for additional information. In this instant filing,
SPP submits its responses to the specific questions raised in the August Letter.

     II.       REQUEST FOR ALTERNATIVE IMPLEMENTATION DATE

As the Commission noted in its August Letter, SPP’s April Filing (as well as its Amended
Filing) requested an effective date of January 1, 2027. SPP now requests an effective date
for its proposed revisions of June 1, 2027, for implementation and planning purposes.19
This requested effective date would render accepted Tariff revisions in place prior to the
2027 Winter Season, which begins on December 1, 2027. However, the revisions would
not be in effect ahead of the 2027 Summer Season. This request may affect SPP’s Open
Access Transmission Tariff Business Practices,20 but it does not affect the proposed Tariff
revisions before the Commission.

     III.      RESPONSE TO AUGUST LETTER

Question 1:

SPP requests an effective date of January 1, 2027 for the tariff records submitted in
the filing and notes that the requested effective date is “subject to additional

       a.     Please explain and provide additional support for SPP’s proposal to
              make its request for an effective date of January 1, 2027, “subject to

Response to Question 1.a:

As described above, SPP requested an original effective date of January 1, 2027. SPP now
requests that the proposed revisions become effective on June 1, 2027. This six-month
delay, however, does not alter SPP’s proposed Tariff language.

In the course of the stakeholder process, a number of Load Responsible Entities (“LREs”)
indicated that implementation in 2027 would be impossible due to “regulatory constructs
and contracts.”23 These LREs requested that implementation be pushed back to 2028 or

2029.24 However, SPP staff conducted analysis regarding the effects of delaying
implementation, and determined that, with a 2028 implementation date (as opposed to a
2027 implementation date), with no cap on load-modifiers,25 the SPP footprint would be
more likely to experience the following in 2027:

     •   9.5 days of EEA1/EEA2 declarations to ensure Operating Reserves in Summer
     •   2.5 days of EEA1/EEA2 declarations to ensure Operating Reserves in Winter
     •   1.8 to 2.5 days of EEA3 where Operating Reserves are unable to be carried in
         Summer
     •   0.8 to 1 days of EEA3 where Operating Reserves are unable to be carried in Winter
     •   0.4 to 0.6 days of firm load shed for balancing in both Summer and Winter
     •   Potential reduction of 1.5 M (2%) MWhrs of available maintenance.26

Therefore, on the one hand, SPP found its footprint faced with potential reliability risks
posed by delayed implementation. On the other hand, with a 2027 implementation date,
some LREs faced potentially impossible timelines. Accordingly, SPP crafted language in
its governing documents (both the Tariff and the Business Practices) intended to mitigate
reliability risks while also recognizing the practicalities of implementation.

With respect to the Tariff, the relevant language begins with the proposed term “Non-
Registered Demand Response Program,” which, under current Tariff language, can be a
“Demand Response Program” or “Non-Controllable and Non-Dispatchable Demand
Response Program.” In essence, a Non-Registered Demand Response Program is a load
modifier. Load modifiers are not registered with SPP. However, an LRE can denote a load

mentions Non-Registered Demand Response Programs on just a few occasions: (1) to
define the term as “A load reduction program that is not a Demand Response Resource or
a Reliability-Registered Demand Response Program”;28 (2) to require that LREs identify
any “projected amount from Non-Registered Demand Response Programs included in the
Peak Demand” in their Workbooks;29 and (3) to include Non-Registered Demand Response
Programs as components of an LRE’s “Peak Demand.”30

In other words, while SPP’s Tariff recognizes Non-Registered Demand Response
Programs (i.e., load modifiers), SPP does not settle based on these programs; SPP does not
commit them; SPP does not dispatch them; and SPP does not have operational visibility
into these programs. Rather, such programs are just another input into an LRE’s Peak
Demand. Indeed, a Non-Registered Demand Response Program is typically established and
administered through an LRE’s own retail tariff. For example, an LRE’s retail tariff or rate
schedule may establish the underlying customer program, such as the interruptible service,
curtailable load, or direct-load control, as well as the LRE’s contractual right to cause or
obtain the load reduction.

The Business Practices provide additional context with respect to the Tariff language.
Specifically, Business Practice 810031 proposes to describe how load modifiers may be

This language reflects that the proposed Tariff language will be implemented prior to 2028.
In light of a proposed 2027 effective date, this language provides details necessary to carry
out the Tariff’s requirements with respect to load modifiers and Peak Demand, specifically
regarding a temporal limitation on how load modifiers serve as inputs into an LRE’s Peak
Demand in 2027, and how the LRE’s pre-season forecast may factor into the initial
assessment of its resource adequacy requirements. In the event that an LRE finds itself
unable to fully utilize the new proposed demand response construct in 2027 (for example,
for regulatory or contractual reasons), such an LRE has the option to utilize the amount of
load modifier which it had previously forecasted in its 2025 Workbook.33 Although the
Business Practices use the term “Pre-Season Requirement” to describe the adjustment, SPP
intends its Business Practices to reflect the use of the Tariff’s proposed Resource Adequacy
Requirement (“RAR”), with the input of the Pre-Season Requirement playing a different
role into that RAR with respect to LREs which adhere to their previously-forecasted load
modifier amounts. Here, an LRE which (1) utilizes this option; and (2) which satisfies its
Pre-Season Requirement will be considered to have satisfied its RAR.

Importantly, this language does not preclude an LRE which did not forecast any load
modifiers (or exceeds its forecasted load modifiers) in its 2025 Workbook from utilizing
load modifiers in 2027. Rather, LREs who (1) forecasted zero load modifiers in their 2025
Workbooks; and (2) utilize load modifiers in 2027 will be considered to have “exceed[ed]
[their] limit,” and therefore their satisfaction (or not) of their Resource Adequacy
Requirements will be independent of their satisfaction (or not) of their Pre-Season
Requirements. Specifically, although the LRE’s forecasting practices and methodology
will be input into how weather normalization is performed (and therefore will be input into

how the Post-Season Net Peak Demand is calculated), whether the LRE demonstrated the
ability to “cover” its pre-season net Peak Demand will not determine whether the LRE has
satisfied its RAR. This is because the new construct is intended, in relevant part, to account
for the effects of load modifiers on the system in excess of what was previously anticipated.
With load modifiers, SPP may have limited assurance that the load reduction will actually
occur when the system needs it, a particular concern with respect to load modifiers that
were not previously forecasted in an LRE’s workbook, and with the amount of large loads
which may come onto the system. Therefore, in the long-term, a post-season analysis is
necessary to guard against the reliability risks posed by the increasing amount of load
modifiers. For example, if an LRE’s gross peak load is 1,000 MW, it could denote 100
MW of load modifier in its Workbook. The forecasted Net Peak Demand is therefore 900
MW. If the Accredited Capacity Planning Reserve Margin (“PRM”) is 16%, this means
that the LRE’s RAR without the load modifier is 1,160 MW, whereas the RAR with the
load modifier is only 1,044 MW. This is appropriate only if that 100 MW actually
disappears at peak—otherwise, reliability concerns could arise.

Finally, the SPP West BAA has no cap on load modifiers. This is because the SPP West
BAA does not generally have a large amount of load modifiers in its footprint, and therefore
SPP staff determined that no cap is warranted at this time. Moreover, LREs in the SPP
West BAA did not submit Workbooks in 2025, and therefore there is no comparable
forecasted amount to utilize.

All that said, to the extent the Commission is concerned that the requirements currently
reflected in SPP’s proposed Business Practices should be set forth in the Tariff, SPP
proposes to incorporate those requirements into the Tariff. Incorporating these provisions
into the Tariff would not alter the functional design, nor would it represent a departure
from the design that stakeholders considered (and which the Regional State Committee and
the Board of Directors approved) prior to the filing of the instant revisions.

Accordingly, if the Commission determines that additional Tariff language is necessary to
address the concern identified in this letter, SPP respectfully requests that the Commission
accept SPP’s proposal subject to SPP submitting a compliance filing incorporating the
relevant Business Practice provisions into the Tariff.

       b. Please explain why it is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory
          or preferential to allow an LRE to continue to have its Post-Season Net
          Peak Demand consider the LRE’s forecast net Peak Demand (rather than
          actual, weather normalized, as otherwise proposed) until the 2028 summer

Response to Question 1.b:

First, the proposal is just and reasonable because an LRE’s weather normalization
methodology is an input into its forecasted Pre-Season Net Peak Demand , which in turn
is input into the Post-Season Net Peak Demand. Therefore, the fact that the Business

Practices set forth a temporary application in the resource adequacy process (for the 2027
Winter Season only) does not substantively alter the Tariff language, but rather acts similar
to other inputs described in the Business Practices.

Specifically, the proposed definition of “Post-Season Net Peak Demand” reads as follows:

               The actual Peak Demand, normalized for weather related
               impacts in accordance with this Attachment AA and SPP
               Business Practices, adjusted to reflect the contract amount of
               Firm Power with another entity as specified in Section 8.2 of
               this Attachment AA.34

“Peak Demand” is defined as,

               The highest demand including a) transmission losses for
               energy, b) the impacts of Non-Controllable and Non-
               Dispatchable Behind-The-Meter Generation, and c) the
               impacts of Non-Registered Demand Response Programs
               measured over a one clock hour period.35

The specifics on how the “highest demand” is determined, along with how to determine
the impact of Non-Registered Demand Response Programs (i.e., load modifiers), is further
described in the Business Practices. Indeed, proposed Section 12.1 of Attachment AA
refers the reader to the Business Practices:

               12.1    The actual Peak Demand shall be adjusted by
                       weather normalization based on the individual
                       LRE’s forecasting practices to determine the Post-
                       Season Net Peak Demand. The Transmission
                       Provider shall apply the weather normalization
                       process, and additional adjustments necessary to
                       determine the Post-Season Net Peak Demand, in
                       accordance with the SPP Business Practices.36

Thus, the Tariff describes that the Post-Season Net Peak Demand is the “actual Peak
Demand” which may be adjusted in accordance with the Business Practices. “Actual” is
not defined. However, “Peak Demand” is defined, in relevant part, as “the highest
demand,” and includes “the impacts of Non-Registered Demand Response Programs…”
The “impacts” of Non-Registered Demand Response Programs (i.e., load modifiers) is not
further described in the Tariff. Rather, the Business Practices that, prior to 2028, whether
an LRE chooses to adhere to its forecasted load modifier amount (or not) will impact how
the LRE’s Peak Demand is determined, which in turn will impact whether the LRE is
considered to be resource adequate.

Recently, in Am. Elec. Power Serv. Corp., et al., 184 FERC ¶ 61,207, at P 26 (2023), the
Commission described the rule of reason as follows:

               Whether an item should be placed in a tariff or business
               practices manual is guided by the rule of reason, under which
               provisions that “significantly affect rates, terms, and
               conditions” of service, are readily susceptible of
               specification, and are not generally understood in a
               contractual agreement must be included in the tariff, while
               items better classified as implementation details need not be
               included in a tariff and may be included in the business
               practices manual. As the Commission stated in the
               Complaint Order, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District
               of Columbia Circuit (D.C. Circuit) has recognized that “[i]t
               is obviously left to the Commission, within broad bounds of
               discretion, to give concrete application to this amorphous
               directive.” Furthermore, when applying the rule of reason,
               the Commission assesses not “some absolute prescribed

               standard literally set forth in the statute and regulations[], but
               ... the minimum specificity that the Commission could
               reasonably require.” The D.C. Circuit also recently
               confirmed that “even specifiable practices that significantly
               affect rates need not be included if they are clearly implied
               by the tariff's express terms.”38

Specifically, with respect to the PRM, the Commission found that, although the PRM
“significantly affects rates, terms, and conditions,” “the inclusion of a process used to
determine the Planning Reserve Margin in the Tariff is sufficient to satisfy the rule of
reason.”39 The Commission continued:

               Moreover, the Commission allows the use of a process in
               other contexts, such as for the establishment of inputs that
               significantly    affect    rates     set   in     organized
               markets. Accordingly, we conclude that as long as a tariff
               expressly provides a sufficiently detailed process for
               determining a planning reserve margin, the rule of reason is
               satisfied, and no specific value must be codified in the
               tariff.40

That said, this language means that SPP measures the output within an hour duration

With the addition of the Post-Season Net Peak Demand concept, this means that the highest

Peak Demand hour. However, this is just and reasonable, because resource adequacy
requirements are intended to determine the LRE’s underlying capacity needs for the
applicable season. Thus, although an LRE’s actual Peak Demand could occur during an
extreme temperature event, the policy is specifically designed to take that scenario into
account and to determine what an LRE’s Peak Demand would have been given “normal”
weather conditions. In other words, the policy (1) produces a more representative measure
of demand in any given season; and (2) better aligns with the demand measurement for
purposes of resource adequacy; and (3) reduces arbitrary year-to-year volatility.

weather normalization methodology. SPP will apply this error tolerance, which could be
construed as an “additional adjustment,” in accordance with its Business Practices.

       d.      SPP states that a temporary cap on Non-Registered Demand Response
               Programs is one such additional adjustment to determine Post-Season
               Net Peak Demand. SPP explains that “[w]ith the proposed temporary
               cap, SPP is not changing the requirements set forth in the Tariff—SPP
               is adding a temporal limitation which reflects the forecasts that LREs
               have already submitted to SPP via their 2027 Workbooks, as set forth

               in the Tariff.”75


               i.      Please explain under what circumstances the Non-Registered
                       Demand Response Program cap will be applied to LREs and
                       why the Non-Registered Demand Response Program cap is just
                       and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.
                       Please identify any relevant current or proposed Tariff
                       provisions.

Response to Question 3.d.i:

With respect to the Tariff, the relevant language begins with the proposed term “Non-
Registered Demand Response Program,” which, under current Tariff language, can be a
“Demand Response Program” or “Non-Controllable and Non-Dispatchable Demand
Response Program” In essence, a Non-Registered Demand Response Program is a load
modifier. Load modifiers are not registered with SPP. However, an LRE can denote a load
modifier in its seasonal Workbook in order to reduce its Peak Demand.76 The Tariff
mentions Non-Registered Demand Response Programs on just a few occasions: (1) to
define the term as “A load reduction program that is not a Demand Response Resource or
a Reliability-Registered Demand Response Program”;77 (2) to require that LREs identify
any “projected amount from Non-Registered Demand Response Programs included in the
Peak Demand” in their Workbooks;78 and (3) to include Non-Registered Demand Response
Programs as components of an LRE’s “Peak Demand.”79

In other words, while SPP’s Tariff recognizes Non-Registered Demand Response
Programs (i.e., load modifiers), SPP does not settle based on these programs; SPP does not
commit them; SPP does not dispatch them; and SPP does not have operational visibility
into these programs. Rather, such programs are just another input into an LRE’s Peak
Demand. Indeed, a Non-Registered Demand Response Program is typically established and
administered through an LRE’s own retail tariff. For example, an LRE’s retail tariff or rate
schedule may establish the underlying customer program, such as the interruptible service,



75
       SPP Answer at 11 (citing Proposed Tariff, Att. AA, § 11.2(8)).
76
       Proposed Tariff, Att. AA, § 11.2.
77
       Proposed Tariff, Att. AA, § 2.0 (Definition of “Demand Non-Registered Demand
       Response Program”).
78
       Proposed Tariff, Att. A, § 11.2(8).
79
       Proposed Tariff, Att. A, § 2.0 (revised definition of “Peak Demand”).

September 18, 2026
Page 29


curtailable load, direct-load control, as well as the LRE’s contractual right to cause or
obtain the load reduction.

The Business Practices provide additional context with respect to the Tariff language.
Specifically, Business Practice 8100 describes how load modifiers may be considered in
an LRE’s forecast prior to 2028:

          4. Prior to implementation in the 2028 Summer Season, 2,298.5
             MW of Non-Registered Demand Response Programs that are
             controllable by the applicable LRE is assigned to LREs in the
             SPP East Balancing Authority Area. This amount is based on
             the forecasted Non-Registered Demand Response submitted
             by LREs in the 2025 Workbook for the 2027 Summer Season.
             Each LRE will be assigned a portion of the amount to its
             respective 2027 forecasted amount. An LRE that did not
             submit a forecast for the 2027 Summer Season will not be
             assigned a portion of the 2,298.5 MW. For an LRE that
             adheres to its respective amount, any Deficiency Payments
             and allocation of revenues will be determined on its Pre-
             Season Requirement. However, in the event an LRE chooses
             to exceed its limit for the 2027 Summer Season, the LRE will
             be allocated Deficiency Payments and revenues assessed on
             its Resource Adequacy Requirement.

              Prior to the 2028 Summer Season, LREs in the SPP West
              Balancing Authority Area will not have a cap on Non-
              Registered Demand Response Programs, and Deficiency
              Payments and allocation of revenues will be determined on
              their Pre-Season Requirement.80

This language reflects that the proposed Tariff language will be implemented prior to 2028.
In light of a proposed 2027 effective date, this language provides details necessary to carry
out the Tariff’s requirements with respect to load modifiers and Peak Demand, specifically
regarding a temporal limitation on how load modifiers serve as inputs into an LRE’s Peak
Demand prior to 2028, and how the LRE’s pre-season forecast may factor into the initial
assessment of its resource adequacy requirements. In the event that an LRE finds itself
unable to fully utilize the new proposed construct in 2027 (for example, for regulatory or
contractual reasons), such an LRE has the option to utilize the amount of load modifier
which it had previously forecast in its 2025 Workbook. Although the Business Practices
use the term “Pre-Season Requirement” to describe the adjustment, SPP intends its
Business Practices to reflect the use of the Tariff’s proposed RAR, with the input of the


80
       See Attachment 1, Business Practice 8100.
 The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese
September 18, 2026
Page 30


Pre-Season Requirement playing a different role into that RAR with respect to LREs which
adhere to their previously-forecasted load modifier amounts. Here, an LRE which (1)
utilizes this option; and (2) which can “cover” its pre-season Net Peak Demand will be
considered to have satisfied its RAR.

Importantly, this language does not preclude an LRE which did not forecast any load
modifiers (or which exceeds its forecasted load modifiers) in its 2025 Workbook from
utilizing load modifiers in 2027. Rather, LREs who (1) forecasted zero load modifiers in
their 2025 Workbooks; and (2) utilize load modifiers in 2027 will be considered to have
“exceed[ed] [their] limit,” and therefore their satisfaction (or not) of their Resource
Adequacy Requirements will be independent of their satisfaction (or not) of their Pre-
Season Requirements. Specifically, although the LRE’s forecasting practices and
methodology will be input into how weather normalization is performed (and therefore will
be input into how the Post-Season Net Peak Demand is calculated), whether the LRE
demonstrated the ability to “cover” its pre-season net Peak Demand will not determine
whether the LRE has satisfied its RAR. This is because the new construct is intended, in
relevant part, to account for the effects of load modifiers on the system in excess of what
was previously anticipated. With load modifiers, SPP may have limited assurance that the
load reduction will actually occur when the system needs it, a particular concern with
respect to load modifiers that were not forecast in an LRE’s workbook, and with the amount
of large loads which may come onto the system. Therefore, in the long-term, a post-season
analysis is necessary to guard against the reliability risks posed by the increasing amount
of load modifiers. For example, if an LRE’s gross peak load is 1,000 MW, it could denote
100 MW of load modifier in its Workbook. The forecasted Net Peak Demand is therefore
900 MW. If the Accredited Capacity PRM is 16%, this means that the LRE’s RAR without
the load modifier is 1,160 MW, whereas the RAR with the load modifier is only 1,044
MW. This is appropriate only if that 100 MW actually disappears at peak—otherwise, a
reliability problem could arise.

Finally, the SPP West BAA has no cap on load modifiers. This is because the SPP West
BAA does not generally have a large amount of load modifiers in its footprint, and therefore
SPP staff determined that no cap is warranted at this time. Moreover, LREs in the West
BAA did not submit Workbooks in 2025, and therefore there is no comparable forecasted
amount to utilize.

Section 205 of the FPA requires the filing of “all rates and charges for any transmission or
sale” subject to FERC's jurisdiction, and the “classifications, practices, and regulations
affecting such rates and charges.” 16 U.S.C. ¶ 824d(c). The Commission has wide latitude
to determine what practices must be on file, as there is “an infinitude of practices affecting
rates and service.” City of Cleveland v. FERC, 773 F.2d 1368, 1376 (D.C. Cir. 1985).
“[E]ven specifiable practices that significantly affect rates need not be included [in a filed
tariff] if they are clearly implied by the tariffs express terms.” Hecate Energy Greene Cnty.
3 LLC v. FERC, 72 F.4th 1307, 1314 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (citing City of Cleveland, 773 F.2d
at 1376).
 The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese
September 18, 2026
Page 31


The Commission has previously held that implementation details need not be set forth in a
Tariff’s rates, terms, or conditions. For example, the D.C. Circuit's recent Hecate decision
clarified that even a specifiable practice significantly affecting rates need not be included
expressly in a tariff if its express terms “clearly impl[y]” the practice. 81 Here, Attachment
AA to the Tariff sets forth the requirements for load modifiers: (1) an LRE must submit its
load modifiers in its Workbook;82 (2) SPP will make adjustment to the LRE’s peak demand
(implicitly, load modifiers is included in this adjustment);83 (3) an LRE can use load
modifiers to offset its Peak Demand;84 and (4) the Business Practices describe these
parameters in further detail.85 With the proposed temporary cap on load modifiers, SPP is
not changing the requirements set forth in the Tariff—SPP is adding a temporal limitation
which reflects the forecasts that LREs have already submitted to SPP via their Workbooks,
as set forth in the Tariff.86

Relatedly, in a recent capacity accreditation proceeding, the Commission explained that
“PJM should have the flexibility to adjust in consultation with stakeholders” “modeling
assumptions such as weather patterns, load shapes, and resource output profiles.”87 The
Commission noted its prior determination that “‘study assumptions and parameters are
likely to change over time as planners gain experience”’ and “‘[t]hus, rigid specifications
or formulas set out in the Tariff would likely lead to less reliable assessments due to the
inability of planners to adapt to changing circumstances.”’88 Here, as in PJM, rigid
specification in the Tariff of a temporary cap based on LREs’ changing forecasts could be
detrimental. In fact, this has already been seen in action. In February 2026, the revisions
approved by the RSC and the Board contained a 2,152 MW cap within the Business
Practices. However, subsequently, SPP and an LRE discovered an error in that LRE’s
LMDR forecast. Therefore, SPP subsequently revised the cap (to 2,298 MW) to reflect
correction of the error, and this revised cap was approved by the RSC and the Board of
Directors in May 2026. If such a cap were to be placed in the Tariff, then any change in
LREs’ forecasts, or any correction to formulae or calculations, would become much more


81
       Hecate Energy Greene Cnty. 3 LLC v. FERC, 72 F.4th 1307, 1314 (D.C. Cir. 2023).
82
       Proposed Tariff, Att. AA, § 11.2.

       Proposed Tariff, Att. AA, § 12.1.

       PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 175 FERC ¶ 61,084, at P 66 (2021).
88
       Id. P 65 (quoting Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 136 FERC ¶ 61,050 at P 37).
 The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese
September 18, 2026
Page 32


difficult to remedy, and would necessitate an otherwise unnecessary filing with the
Commission. Therefore, it is beneficial for SPP to retain discretion—within Tariff
boundaries—to adjust load modifier parameters, a discretion which “rigid specification”
would otherwise hamper. See PacifiCorp, 192 FERC ¶ 61,197, P 315 (2025) (“Here, we
find that discussions about the specific historical load data or methodologies—including
the three-year historical load data contemplated in PacifiCorp's draft business practice
manuals and matters of how to adjust load forecasts—are appropriately managed in its
business practice development.”); Hecate Energy Greene Cnty. 3 LLC v. Central Hudson
Gas & Electric Corp, et al., 177 FERC ¶ 61,121, at P 48 (2021) (“We continue to find that
[New York Independent System Operator, Inc.’s (“NYISO”)] existing OATT provisions
that describe how NYISO establishes and uses the Base Case provide sufficient notice to
customers that transmission owners will provide information to NYISO about which
projects need to be modeled in the Base Case. While the Base Case significantly impacts
rates, terms, and conditions of service, we find the ‘inclusion practice’ is an implementation
detail that simply describes how one particular utility identifies information that the
NYISO OATT requires to be communicated to NYISO in order to establish the Base Case.
Further, as noted above, updates communicated by transmission owners, such as the fact
that the [New York State Standardized Interconnection Requirements (“NYSSIR”)]
Projects have become firm for purposes of inclusion in the Base Case, are only one of
potentially many updates that could be provided in accordance with the existing OATT.
Thus, the Commission reasonably determined in the June 2021 Order that “NYISO's
existing OATT already provides for the use of the ‘inclusion practice - i.e., by allowing
NYISO to use information from the transmission owner in order to develop the Base Case
for the interconnecting project's facilities study.’”) (internal citations omitted); City of
Cleveland, Ohio v. FERC, 773 F.2d 1368, 1376 (D.C. Cir. 1985) (“[T]here is an infinitude
of practices affecting rates and service….”).

All that said, and to reiterate, to the extent the Commission is concerned that the
requirements currently reflected in SPP’s proposed Business Practices should be set forth
in the Tariff, SPP proposes to incorporate those requirements into the Tariff. Incorporating
these provisions into the Tariff would not alter the functional design, nor would it represent
a departure from the design that stakeholders considered (and which the Regional State
Committee and the Board approved) prior to the filing of the instant revisions.

Accordingly, if the Commission determines that additional Tariff language is necessary to
address the concerns identified in this letter, SPP respectfully requests that the Commission
accept SPP’s proposal subject to SPP submitting, a compliance filing incorporating the
relevant Business Practice provisions into the Tariff.
 The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese
September 18, 2026
Page 33


               ii.    Please explain the duration for which this proposed temporary
                      cap will apply to LREs and under what circumstances it will be
                      removed. Please identify any relevant current or proposed
                      Tariff provisions.

Response to Question 3.d.ii:

The cap on load modifiers will apply to LREs which choose to be bound by the cap until
the 2028 Summer Season. This is because a number of LREs indicated that they will be
unable to procure the necessary regulatory approvals and negotiate any applicable contracts
prior to the 2028 summer season. The cap will cease to exist after the 2027 Winter Season
(which begins December 1, 2027). Except to the extent the Tariff refers the reader to the
Business Practices, the Tariff does not address the cap or its expiration.

Question 4:

SPP proposes to define Firm Service Level as the “expected load measured over a one
clock hour period after the [DRR] or [RRDRP] has been deployed to its Net
Generating Capability.”89 SPP further proposes to use the Firm Service Level to
determine DRR and RRDRP Accredited Capacity;90 moreover, qualified DRRs and
RRDRPs “shall be capable of maintaining their Firm Service Level for a minimum of
four (4) continuous hours.”91 Please explain how the Firm Service Level is calculated
and whether this calculation is the same or different based on resource type (i.e.,
DRR, RRDRP). Please identify any relevant current or proposed Tariff provisions.

Response to Question 4:

A resource’s Firm Service Level is calculated based on the resource’s expected load after
it has been deployed to its Net Generating Capability.92 “Net Generating Capability” is
currently defined in Attachment AA, in relevant part, as “A resource’s gross maximum
output sustained over a one-hour period, demonstrated with a capability test….”93 The
determination of the Firm Service Level differs by resource type to the extent that the
determination of Net Generating Capability test differs by resource type.

The capability test applicable to the Net Generating Capability is explained in Section 7.1
of SPP’s Planning Criteria,94 and varies depending on the resource type (i.e., thermal unit,

Planning Criteria, entitled, “Testing Requirements and Accreditation for Demand
Response Resources and RRDRPs,” which will describe the specific capability test
applicable to DRRs and RRDRPs:

                      will be required to update the available capacity of

                      tested. Submitting zero available capacity will result
                      in a reschedule of the Capability Test.
                   4. SPP operations staff will then direct the Market

                      the Capability Test at any point during the testing
                      period.
                   5. The amount of load reduced during the testing period
                      shall be the demonstrated Net Generating Capability
                      of the Demand Response Resource or RRDRP.
                   6. A Market Participant or Load Responsible Entity is

                      the allotted time.

             deployment may suffice as a Capability Test if it meets the

             The seasonal capability established for a Demand Response
             Resource or RRDRP shall be adjusted in accordance with
             the Demand Response Reporting and Documentation
             Procedures given in the SPP Business Practices. The
             Demand Response Resource or RRDRP’s Net Generating
             Capability shall not be greater than the highest expected load

             peak season but shall only be considered a Capability Test
             during the first year of operation. It shall follow the same

             peak operating season after initial enrollment.

                1. An entity may claim up to 50% of the expected

 The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese
September 18, 2026

                      capability.95
Once the above-described capability test has been conducted, SPP and the applicable
Market Participant may then arrive at the Resource’s Net Generating Capability. Then, the
Firm Service Level is derived from the Net Generating Capability.

From there, proposed Section 7.7(f) of Attachment AA states that a DRR will submit its
Firm Service Level for the applicable season in its Workbook in advance of each Summer
Season and Winter Season. Section 7.8(f) states the same with respect to RRDRPs, and
Section 7.9(f) states the same with respect to Emergency Demand Response Programs. SPP
expects that the Firm Service Level may change from season to season, or year to year, as
the forecasted load provided in the LRE’s Workbook applicable to the demand response
resource or program may change due to load growth or decline.

IV.    CONCLUSION

For all of the reasons discussed in this instant filing, the Commission should accept the
Tariff revisions submitted in this proceeding as just and reasonable. SPP requests that the
Commission issue an order in this proceeding as soon as practicable, but not later than
November 18, 2026, which is sixty (60) days from the date of this filing.

2.0    Definitions


Terms defined herein shall only be applicable to this Attachment AA.


Accredited Capacity
The capacity assigned to a resource after accounting for its Conventional Resource Performance
Adjustment, or Effective Load Carrying Capability Study, or Demand Response Performance
Adjustment results in accordance with this Attachment AA, SPP Planning Criteria, and SPP
Business Practices.


Accredited Capacity Planning Reserve Margin (“Accredited Capacity PRM”)
The enforceable planning reserve margin for both the Summer Season and Winter Season Pre-
Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement as determined pursuant to Section 5.0
of this Attachment AA.


Adjusted Net Peak Load
The Net Peak Load less the a) actual production output of all wind resources in the applicable
SPP Balancing Authority Area and b) actual production output of all solar resources in the
applicable SPP Balancing Authority Area.


Asset Owner
As defined in Attachment AE of this Tariff.


Authorized Outage
Scheduled Resource Outages which are authorized by the Balancing Authority at the time when
the Balancing Authority’s study does not identify any reliability issues with the Scheduled
Resource Outage as outlined in Section 3.1.5.1 of Attachment AE of this Tariff.


Base Planning Reserve Margin (“Base PRM”)
The planning reserve margin as determined in Section 4.0 of this Attachment AA that will be
used as the basis for calculating the Accredited Capacity PRM.
 Behind-The-Meter Generation
As defined in Attachment AE of this Tariff. Behind-The-Meter Generation shall not be qualified
or accredited as Demand Response Capacity in accordance with Attachment AA of this Tariff.


Conservative Operations Demand Response Program
A resource created to model Demand Response Load reduction associated with controllable load
that is 1) capable of being deployed at the direction of a Transmission Provider, Load
Responsible Entity, or a Market Participant and 2) available to respond during a) conservative
operations advisories, b) any level of EEA Emergency Conditions and c) Local Reliability
Issues.


Conventional Resource Performance Adjustment
The historical performance adjustment for conventional resources using the combination of a
modified demand Equivalent Forced Outage Rate (“EFORd”) method and Equivalent Forced
Outage Factor (“EFOF”) method adjusted for Incremental Outage Impact in accordance with this
Attachment AA and the SPP Business Practices. A resource’s EFOF shall only be considered
during the Winter Season. Conventional resources are defined as thermal fuel type resources,
pump storage hydroelectric resources, and hydroelectric resources with reservoir storage
capability not subject to hourly river flow limitations similar to run-of-river hydro.


Deficiency Payment
A payment by a Market Participant when one or more of its LREs has not met the Resource
Adequacy Requirement as calculated in accordance with Section 14.0 of this Attachment AA.


Deliverable Capacity
The Accredited Capacity available for a Resource that is determined in either a Summer Season
Deliverability Study or a Winter Season Deliverability Study.


Demand Response Capacity
 The Accredited Capacity of a Demand Response Resource or Reliability Registered Demand
Response Program.


Demand Response Performance Adjustment
The historical performance adjustment for Demand Response Resource or Reliability Registered
Demand Response Program using the method(s) in accordance with this Attachment AA and the
SPP Business Practices.


Demand Response Resource
As defined in Attachment AE of this Tariff.


Demand Response Program
Measurable load reduction program(s) capable of being controlled or dispatched by a Load
Responsible Entity, a Market Participant, or the Transmission Provider.


Electric Storage Resource
As defined in Part I, Section 1 of this Tariff.


Emergency Condition
As defined in Part I, Section 1 of this Tariff.


Emergency Demand Response Program
A resource created to model Demand Response Load reduction associated with controllable load
that is (1) capable of being deployed at the direction of a Transmission Provider, Load
Responsible Entity, or a Market Participant; and (2) available to respond during (a) any level of
EEA Emergency Conditions and (b) Local Reliability Issues.


Energy Emergency Alert (“EEA”)
As defined by applicable NERC Reliability Standards.


Firm Capacity
 The Accredited Capacity of commercially operable generating units, or portions of generating
units, adjusted to reflect purchases and sales of capacity with another party, and that is
deliverable with firm transmission service to the LRE’s load.


Firm Power
Power purchases and sales deliverable with firm transmission service to serve the LRE’s load
with capacity, energy, and planning reserves, that must be continuously available in a manner
comparable to power delivered to native load customers.


Firm Service Level
The expected load measured over a one clock hour period after the Demand Response Resource
or Reliability Registered Demand Response Program has been deployed to its Net Generating
Capability.


Generator Owner
The Asset Owner of a Resource.


Incremental Outage Impact
The incremental impact of simultaneous conventional resource forced outages in excess of the
normally modeled forced outages experienced during timeframes of extreme temperatures from
the LOLE Study. This value shall be assessed in accordance with the LOLE Study scope and
SPP Business Practices. Incremental Outage Impact shall only be considered during the Winter
Season.


Jointly Owned Unit
As defined in Attachment AE of this Tariff.


Load Responsible Entity (“LRE”)
An Asset Owner with registered load in the Integrated Marketplace.


Local Reliability Issue
 As defined in Attachment AE of this Tariff.


Market Participant
As defined in Attachment AE of this Tariff.


Net Generating Capability
A resource’s gross maximum output sustained over a one-hour period, demonstrated with a
capability test, reduced by any power used for unitresource auxiliaries, and modified for
environmental, seasonal, operational, and fuel limitations. For resources qualified as internal to
the SPP Balancing Authority Areas, the resources shall meet the testing requirements in
accordance with the SPP Planning Criteria. Resources qualified as external to the SPP Balancing
Authority Areas shall adhere to the testing requirements of the Balancing Authority where the
resource(s) is located.


Net Peak Demand
The forecasted Peak Demand less the a) projected impacts of a Demand Response Program and
b) adjusted to reflect the contract amount of Firm Power with another entity as specified in
Section 8.2 of this Attachment AA.


Net Peak Load
The actual Peak Demand less the actual impacts of a Demand Response Resource and Reliability
Registered Demand Response Program.


Non-Controllable and Non-Dispatchable Behind-The-Meter Generation
Behind-The-Meter Generation resources that are non-controllable and non-dispatchable by the
Transmission Provider, Market Participant, or the LRE.


Non-ControllableRegistered and Non-Dispatchable Demand Response Programs
A load reduction program that is not a Demand Response Resource or Reliability Registered
Demand Response Programs that are non-controllable and non-dispatchable by the Transmission
Provider, Market Participant, or the LRE.
 Outage
As defined in Attachment AE of this Tariff.


Peak Demand
The highest demand including a) transmission losses for energy, b) the projected impacts of
Non-Controllable and Non-Dispatchable Behind-The-Meter Generation, and c) the projected
impacts of Non-ControllableRegistered and Non-Dispatchable Demand Response Programs
measured over a one clock hour period.


Post-Season Net Peak Demand
The actual Peak Demand, normalized for weather related impacts in accordance with this
Attachment AA and SPP Business Practices, adjusted to reflect the contract amount of Firm
Power with another entity as specified in Section 8.2 of this Attachment AA.


Pre-Season Net Peak Demand
The forecasted Peak Demand adjusted to reflect the contract amount of Firm Power with another
entity as specified in Section 8.2 of this Attachment AA.


Pre-Season Requirement
The Pre-Season Requirement for both the Summer Season and Winter Season for each LRE is
determined pursuant to Section 5.0 of this Attachment AA.


Reliability Registered Demand Response Program (“RRDRP”)
Conservative Operations Demand Response Programs or Emergency Demand Response
Programs.


Resource
As defined in Part I, Section 1 of this Tariff.


Resource Adequacy Requirement
 The Resource Adequacy Requirement for both the Summer Season and Winter Season for each
LRE is determined pursuant to Section 5.0 of this Attachment AA.


Scheduled Resource Outage
As defined in Attachment AE of this Tariff.


SPP Balancing Authority Areas
As defined in Part I, Section 1 of this Tariff.


SPP East Balancing Authority Area
As defined in Part I, Section 1 of this Tariff.


SPP West Balancing Authority Area
As defined in Part I, Section 1 of this Tariff.


Summer Season
June 1st through September 30th of each year.


Undeployed Availability
Capacity from a Demand Response Resource or Reliability Registered Demand Response
Program available to the Transmission Provider for deployment that was not deployed as
determined in accordance with the SPP Business Practices.


Winter Season
December 1st through March 31st of each year.


Workbook
An electronic tool provided by the Transmission Provider which is used by an LRE or Generator
Owner to submit information to the Transmission Provider for the purposes of administering this
Attachment AA.       The electronic tool will allow an LRE or Generator Owner to update
 information contained in a previously submitted Workbook for purposes of satisfying its
requirements under Attachment AA.
 3.0   Roles and Responsibilities


3.1   Generator Owner and Load Responsible Entity
             Except as provided in Section 3.1(1) of this Attachment AA, the roles and
      responsibilities of the LRE and Generator Owner are separate and distinct from the other
      under this Attachment AA. An entity may be an LRE, a Generator Owner, or both. For
      an entity that is both an LRE and Generator Owner, the Transmission Provider shall
      recognize the rights, roles, and responsibilities as separate and distinct functions.
      (1)    An LRE that is also a Generator Owner shall access its Workbook pursuant to the
             provisions of Section 9.3(b) of this Attachment AA but shall be considered an
             LRE for Workbook reporting purposes, and all excess capacity of the Generator
             Owner shall be considered LRE Excess Capacity for purposes of Resource
             Adequacy Assurance as described in Section 14.0 of this Attachment AA.
      (2)    An entity that serves load in both the SPP East Balancing Authority Area and the
             SPP West Balancing Authority Area must separately designate the load assigned
             to the SPP East Balancing Authority Area and the load assigned to the SPP West
             Balancing Authority Area for their compliance obligations pursuant to
             Attachment AA.
      (3)    A Generator Owner that that operates Resources in both the SPP East Balancing
             Authority Area and the SPP West Balancing Authority Area must separately
             qualify and assign its Resources to the SPP East Balancing Authority Area and its
             Resources to the SPP West Balancing Authority Area for their compliance
             obligations pursuant to Attachment AA.


3.2   Market Participant and Load Responsible Entity
      (1)    An LRE may be a Market Participant or can engage a third- party Market
             Participant to represent it. If an LRE refuses to either (a) become a Market
             Participant or (b) engage a third- party Market Participant to represent it, the
             Transmission Provider shall file an unexecuted Market Participant Agreement
             with the Commission pursuant to Section 2.2(6) of Attachment AE of this Tariff.
 (2)   A Market Participant that represents an LRE under Attachment AH of this Tariff
      is the entity responsible under this Attachment AA to ensure the LRE has
      sufficient capacity to meet the Pre-Season Requirement and the LRE’s
      compliance with the Resource Adequacy Requirement.
      (a)    The relationship between a Market Participant and its LRE, as established
             under Attachment AH by February 1st, will be considered fixed for the
             upcoming Summer Season for enforcement of the Summer Season Pre-
             Season Requirement and enforcement of the Summer Season Resource
             Adequacy Requirement.

      (b)    The relationship between a Market Participant and its LRE, as established
             under Attachment AH by August 1st, will be considered fixed for the
             upcoming Winter Season for enforcement of the Winter Season Pre-
             Season Requirement and enforcement of the Winter Season Resource
             Adequacy Requirement.


(3)   The Market Participant is responsible to ensure its LRE(s) provides the necessary
      data to allow the Transmission Provider to verify its LRE has sufficient capacity
      to meet the Pre-Season Requirement and its LRE(s)’ compliance with the
      Resource Adequacy Requirement.
(4)   An LRE shall submit all necessary data to the Transmission Provider either
      directly or through the LRE’s Market Participant.
(5)   A Market Participant may aggregate the forecasted Peak Demand of multiple
      LREs whose load assets are served by a common set of Designated Resources or a
      Firm Power transaction between the LREs. In such case, the Market Participant
      shall be considered the LRE for the aggregated demand and, for purposes of
      compliance with this Attachment AA, the Market Participant’s forecasted Peak
      Demand shall be used to calculate a Pre-Season Requirement and the actual Peak
      Demand shall be used to calculate a Resource Adequacy Requirement separately
      for the aggregated load assets in each SPP Balancing Authority Area.
       (6)   The Market Participant is responsible for any deficient capacity needed to be
            sufficient for the applicable year’sseason’s Resource Adequacy Requirement
            through a Deficiency Payment incurred by the LRE(s) it represents.


3.3   Procedures for Assignment of Market Participant Obligations
      (1)   A Market Participant may assign its duties, obligations and responsibilities for an
            LRE under this Attachment AA, but only to another Market Participant. A non-
            Market Participant must become a Market Participant prior to accepting an
            assignment.
      (2)   Assignor Market Participant shall be responsible to negotiate and contract with
            another Market Participant for the assignment of its duties, obligations, and
            responsibilities with respect to the LRE. A valid assignment must be in writing,
            bilaterally executed by both parties, and the assignee Market Participant shall
            affirmatively accept the duties, obligations, and responsibilities of the assignor
            Market Participant under this Attachment AA.
      (3)   For the Summer Season, the assignor Market Participant shall provide copies of
            the assignment to the Transmission Provider prior to February 1st of each
            calendar year. In the event the demonstration of such assignment does not occur
            prior to February 1st of each calendar year, the Transmission Provider shall not be
            required to accept the assignment for the upcoming Summer Season.
      (4)   For the Winter Season, the assignor Market Participant shall provide copies of the
            assignment to the Transmission Provider prior to August 1st of each calendar
            year. In the event the demonstration of such assignment does not occur prior to
            August 1st of each calendar year, the Transmission Provider shall not be required
            to accept the assignment for the upcoming Winter Season.
      (5)   A valid assignment by the assignor Market Participant under this Attachment AA
            does not affect the assignor Market Participant’s status as a Market Participant or
            other rights and obligations it may have under other provisions of this Tariff.
      (6)   Except as otherwise provided in Sections 3.3(7), 3.3(8), and 3.3(9) of this
            Attachment AA, upon demonstration of a valid assignment, Transmission
            Provider will accept the transfer of the LRE to the assignee Market Participant,
       and enforce the provisions of Attachment AA against the assignee Market
      Participant, without recourse against the assignor Market Participant.
(7)   Either party may serve the Transmission Provider with written notice of the
      assignment’s termination.      The Transmission Provider will recognize the
      assignment’s termination if the notice contains a written acknowledgement by
      both parties that the assignment has been terminated. Upon termination of the
      assignment, the duties, obligations, and responsibilities of the Market Participant
      for the transferred LRE under Attachment AA of the Tariff shall immediately
      revert back to assignor Market Participant, unless a replacement assignment that
      meets the requirements of this section is provided to the Transmission Provider.
(8)   Nothing in the Transmission Provider’s acceptance of the assignment shall be
      construed to create or give rise to any liability on the part of the Transmission
      Provider and the parties to the assignment expressly waive any claims that may
      arise in their favor against the Transmission Provider, except as specifically may
      be provided in the Tariff. The Transmission Provider shall be held harmless by
      the parties for any breach of the assignment or dispute between the parties with
      regards to the assignment, and such dispute shall not delay or cancel the financial
      responsibilities of the assignee Market Participant under this Attachment AA.
      Any dispute between the Transmission Provider and either party may be subject
      to the dispute resolution provisions of Section 12 of the Tariff.
(9)   The Transmission Provider shall not be responsible for the actions of any party, or
      have any affirmative duties assigned to the Transmission Provider under the
      assignment. The Transmission Provider’s recognition of the assignment shall not
      be construed as Transmission Provider’s acceptance of the provisions of the
      assignment that may conflict with the Tariff or the Transmission Provider’s
      administration of the Tariff, and specifically, the application of this Attachment
      AA against the assignee Market Participant, or upon termination of the
      assignment, the assignor Market Participant. In the event there exists a conflict
      between a term of the assignment and this Tariff, the provisions of this Tariff
      shall control.
 5.0    Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement


5.1    The Summer Season Pre-Season Requirement is equal to the LRE’s Summer Season Pre-
       Season Net Peak Demand plus its Summer Season Pre-Season Net Peak Demand
       multiplied by the Accredited Capacity PRM for the Summer Season of the applicable
       SPP Balancing Authority Area for the LRE. The Winter Season Pre-Season Requirement
       is equal to the LRE’s Winter Season Pre-Season Net Peak Demand plus its Winter
       Season Pre-season Net Peak Demand multiplied by the Accredited Capacity PRM for the
       Winter Season of the applicable SPP Balancing Authority Area for the LRE.

       (1)    The Pre-Season Net Peak Demand shall be determined by the applicable LRE or
              Market Participant and submitted in the Workbook in accordance with this
              Attachment AA.

       (2)    An LRE that resolves its capacity deficiency for the purpose of meeting the
              Summer Season Pre-Season Requirement by May 15th and resolves its capacity
              deficiency for the purpose of meeting the Winter Season Pre-Season Requirement
              by November 15th of the applicable year will be considered to have sufficient
              capacity to meet the Pre-Season Requirement.

       (3)    The LRE shall have sufficient firm transmission service from Designated
              Resources, resources associated with Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service,
              and other resources with firm transmission service for the designated amount for
              meeting its Summer Season Pre-Season Net Peak Demand and Winter Season
              Pre-season Net Peak Demand.

5.12   The Summer Season Resource Adequacy Requirement is equal to the LRE’s Summer
       Season Post-Season Net Peak Demand plus its Summer Season Post-Season Net Peak
       Demand multiplied by the Accredited Capacity PRM for the Summer Season of the
       applicable SPP Balancing Authority Area for the LRE. The Winter Season Post-Season
       Resource Adequacy Requirement is equal to the LRE’s Winter Season Post-Season Net
       Peak Demand plus its Winter Season Net Peak Demand multiplied by the Accredited
        Capacity PRM for the Winter Season of the applicable SPP Balancing Authority Area for
       the LRE.

       (1)    The Post-Season Net Peak Demand shall be determined by the Transmission
              Provider in accordance with Section 12 of this Attachment AA.

       (12)   The LRE is responsible to meet the Resource Adequacy Requirement for the
              Summer Season and Winter Season or pay for any deficiencyt capacity needed to
              be sufficientcompliant with for the applicable year’s Resource Adequacy
              Requirement through a Deficiency Payment as calculated in accordance with
              Section 14.0 of this Attachment AA.

       (2)    The LRE shall have sufficient firm transmission service from Designated
              Resources, resources associated with Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service,
              and other resources with firm transmission service for the designated amount for
              meeting its Summer Season Net Peak Demand and Winter Season Net Peak
              Demand.

5.23   The Deliverable Capacity, or Firm Capacity, or Demand Response Capacity utilized by
       an LRE to meet the Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement may
       not be included in the Deliverable Capacity, or Firm Capacity, or Demand Response
       Capacity utilized by another LRE to meet the Pre-Season Requirement and Resource
       Adequacy Requirement. Deliverable Capacity or Firm Capacity that is contracted to
       other entities shall not be available to the LRE that is transferring the Deliverable
       Capacity or Firm Capacity for compliance with the Pre-Season Requirement and
       Resource Adequacy Requirement. Demand Response Capacity qualified to meet an
       LRE’s Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement shall only be
       available to the LRE that is submitting the corresponding load of the Demand Response
       Resource or RRDRP as Peak Demand in its Workbook.

       (1)    Firm Capacity qualified in accordance with this Attachment AA from Behind-
              The-Meter Generation that is not registered in the Integrated Marketplace shall
              have its capacity adjusted in determination of the Resource Adequacy
               Requirement in accordance with the SPP Business Practices when assessing the
              LRE’s Post Season Net Peak Demand.

5.4    The Transmission Provider shall use the Deliverable Capacity, Firm Capacity, Firm
       Power, or Demand Response Capacity qualified to meet an LRE’s Pre-Season
       Requirement to assess such LRE’s compliance with the Resource Adequacy
       Requirement.


5.35   If an LRE serves load both internal and external to the SPP Balancing Authority Areas,
       compliance with the Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement
       contained in this Attachment AA is not intended to affect an LRE’s obligation to
       maintain distinct and separate amounts of Resources to cover its applicable planning
       reserve obligation for its load located external to the SPP Balancing Authority Areas.
       Load and Resources that are pseudo-tied or dynamically scheduled into either of the SPP
       Balancing Authority Areas shall be considered internal for purposes of determining the
       Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement.

5.46   The Base PRM for the Summer Season and Winter Season established in accordance
       with Section 4.0 of this Attachment AA will be used as a basis for calculating a Summer
       Season Accredited Capacity PRM and Winter Season Accredited Capacity PRM of each
       of the SPP Balancing Authority Areas by applying the Accredited Capacity for the
       applicable season in accordance with this Attachment AA and SPP Planning Criteria. The
       Summer Season Accredited Capacity PRM will be utilized to determine the Pre-Season
       Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement for the Summer Season and the
       Winter Season Accredited Capacity PRM will be utilized to determine the Pre-Season
       Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement for the Winter Season.
 6.0   Expectation of Resource Availability

            An LRE or a Generator Owner must only submit Deliverable Capacity, or Firm
      Capacity, or Demand Response Capacity for the capacity of a Resource it expects will be
      available for the duration of the applicable period, which is June 15th through September
      15th for the Summer Season and December 15th through March 15th for the Winter
      Season, unless the Resource receives an Authorized Outage(s) as described in Section
      11.3 of this Attachment AA. The Balancing Authority studies Authorized Outages
      pursuant to Section 3.1.5 of Attachment AE of this Tariff. To ensure availability and
      readiness to perform, certain measures, consistent with Good Utility Practice, must be
      performed subject to the following provisions:

      (1)   The LRE must have no knowledge, consistent with Good Utility Practice, that a
            Resource included in the Workbook for meeting its Pre-Season Requirement and
            Resource Adequacy Requirement will become unavailable unless it has received
            an Authorized Outage(s) prior to inclusion in the Workbook. Unless a Resource
            has received an Authorized Outage(s), the LRE must have made reasonable efforts
            to obtain the knowledge necessary to determine whether a Resource it has included
            in the Workbook for meeting its Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy
            Requirement will become unavailable during the applicable season.

      (2)   The LRE and Generator Owner must not schedule or plan for the Resource’s
            capacity to become unavailable due to an Outage during the applicable season
            without Balancing Authority approval and authorization.

      (3)   The LRE must reflect in its Workbook any Outage that affects the Resource’s
            capacity by the Workbook submittal deadline as specified in Section 11.3 of this
            Attachment AA.

      (4)   The LRE may reflect the entire capacity of the Resource in its Workbook in order
            to meet its Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement if the
            Resource receives an Authorized Outage(s) prior to the Workbook submittal
            deadline as specified in Section 11.3 of this Attachment AA and continues to have
 the Authorized Outage(s) for the Resource on February 15th for the Summer
Season or August 15th for the Winter Season.

7.1   An LRE or Generator Owner with Deliverable Capacity from resources internal to the

      Summer Season and Winter Season by:
      (a)    registering the Resource in the Integrated Marketplace;
      (b)    submitting, or causing to be submitted, to the Transmission Provider the current
             Operational Test results as performed in accordance with the SPP Planning
             Criteria; and
      (c)    submitting, or causing to be submitted, to the Transmission Provider the current
             Capability Test results as performed in accordance with the SPP Planning
             Criteria.


7.2   An LRE or Generator Owner with Firm Capacity from a resource(s) internal to the SPP
      Balancing Authority Areas shall qualify such capacity in the Workbook for each Summer
      Season and Winter Season by:
      (a)    demonstrating the resource(s) is (i) registered in the Integrated Marketplace or (ii)
             listed as a Designated Resource in the Network Integration Transmission Service
             Agreement;
      (b)    submitting, or causing to be submitted, to the Transmission Provider the current
             Operational Test results as performed in accordance with the SPP Planning
             Criteria;
      (c)    submitting, or causing to be submitted, to the Transmission Provider the current
             Capability Test results as performed in accordance with the SPP Planning
             Criteria; and
      (d)    demonstrating that there is firm transmission service from the internal resource(s)
             to the LRE’s load.

             resource(s) is located;
      (c)    demonstrating that there is firm transmission service from the external resource(s)
             to the LRE’s load; and
      (d)    attesting that any external capacity being identified is not otherwise being used as

 8.0   Qualification and Verification of Power Purchase Agreements



8.1   An LRE or Generator Owner shall provide the Transmission Provider a copy of the
      power purchase agreement(s) to enable the Transmission Provider to verify the
      Deliverable Capacity, Firm Capacity, or Firm Power and to confirm compliance with this
      Attachment AA. On a prospective basis, the LRE or Generator Owner shall only submit
      a copy of a new or modified agreement(s).

      (1)    Any redacted versions of a power purchase agreement submitted by an LRE or
             Generator Owner shall contain sufficient information to allow the Transmission
             Provider to verify compliancesufficiency with the Pre-Season Requirement and
             compliance with the Resource Adequacy Requirement.

      (2)    An LRE or Generator Owner with a power purchase agreement that does not
             identify the specific resource(s) shall identify each resource that is available or
             partially available through an attestation supporting the power purchase
             agreement.
      (3)    A power purchase agreement used to meet the Pre-Season Requirement and
             Resource Adequacy Requirement shall be limited to the Accredited Capacity of
             the resource(s) identified in the power purchase agreement or identified in
             accordance with Section 8.1 of this Attachment AA.


8.2   When the purchaser and seller are both LREs, a power purchase agreement that qualifies
      as Firm Power shall result in a Pre-Season Net Peak Demand and Post-Season Net Peak
      Demand adjustment of the obligation for capacity and planning reserves from the
      purchaser to the seller. The purchaser shall deduct the purchased contract amount from
      its Pre-Season Net Peak Demand and the seller shall add the amount to its Pre-Season
      Net Peak Demand. Likewise, the Transmission Provider shall deduct the purchased
      contract amount from the purchaser’s Post-Season Net Peak Demand and shall add the
      amount to the seller’s Post-Season Net Peak Demand. The responsibility to maintain the
      Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement shall transfer from the
      purchaser to the seller.
 8.3   When the seller is not an LRE, a power purchase agreement that qualifies as Firm Power
      shall not result in a Pre-Season Net Peak Demand and Post-Season Net Peak Demand
      adjustment and the purchaser will remain responsible for the Pre-Season Requirement
      and Resource Adequacy Requirement for load served by the agreement. The purchaser
      shall not deduct the purchased contract amount from its Pre-Season Net Peak Demand;
      however, the purchaser may reflect as Firm Capacity the contract amount of the
      agreement plus the purchaser’s Accredited Capacity PRM for the applicable season
      multiplied by the contract amount. Likewise, the Transmission Provider shall not adjust
      the purchaser’s Post-Season Net Peak Demand for the contracted amount.             Firm
      transmission service is only required for the contract amount.


8.4   When the purchaser is not an LRE, a power purchase agreement that qualifies as Firm
      Power shall result in a Firm Capacity transaction for load served by the agreement. The
      seller, who is an LRE, shall not include the purchased contract amount in its Pre-Season
      Net Peak Demand; however, the seller shall reflect as Firm Capacity the contract amount
      of the agreement plus the seller’s Accredited Capacity PRM for the applicable season
      multiplied by the contract amount. Likewise, the Transmission Provider shall not adjust
      the seller’s Post-Season Net Peak Demand for the contracted amount. Firm transmission
      service is only required for the contract amount.


8.5   A power purchase agreement executed prior to July 1, 2018 will continue to be defined
      and qualified as Firm Power if it does not include provisions permitting the seller to
      interrupt deliveries thereunder for reasons other than Force Majeure (as defined in
      Section 10.1 of this Tariff) or uncured defaults. All other power purchase agreements
      must specifically meet the definition of Firm Power.


8.6   An LRE may arrange for short-term capacity to provide a part of its Firm Capacity or
      short-term Firm Power to reduce a portion of its Pre-Season Net Peak Demand or Post-
      Season Net Peak Demand for the Summer Season Net Peak Demand or Winter Season
      Net Peak Demand, subject to the following provisions:
       (1)    Such short-term capacity or short-term Firm Power shall be available for a
             minimum of four consecutive months, starting either June 1st or December 1st;
      (2)    The amount of short-term Firm Capacity or short-term Firm Power purchased in
             aggregate shall not exceed 25% of an LRE’s applicable Pre-Season Net Peak
             Demand and Post-Season Net Peak Demand; and
      (3)    If the seller under a short-term Firm Power agreement is not an LRE, then the
             purchaser under the short-term Firm Power agreement will remain responsible for
             any Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement for load
             served under the short-term Firm Power agreement.

      confidentiality of information received pursuant to Section 8 of this Attachment AA
      when such information is so designated as “confidential” and if such designation is
      reasonable, except to the extent required by this Tariff, by regulatory or judicial order, by
