Attachment 1
SPP Business Practices
              Business Practice 8100
Resource Adequacy requirements and Accreditation
Details for Demand Response Programs and Behind-
               The-Meter Generation
 The purpose of this business practice is to further define the requirements and accreditation
details for Demand Response Programs and behind-the-meter generation less than 10 MW, and
address whether each is treated as a modifier (offset) of an LRE’s load or as resource capacity
for purposes of meeting the Pre-Season Requirement and Resource Adequacy Requirement and
Winter Season Obligation in Attachment AA for both SPP East Balancing Authority Area (SPP
East BAA) and SPP West Balancing Authority Area (SPP West BAA).

CONTENTS

1   Demand Response ProgramsDefinitions
2   Demand Response Resource and RRDRP
    2.1 Identification Requirements
    2.2 Program Identification Timeline
    2.3 Demand Response Reporting and Documentation
    2.4 Emergency Demand Response Limit
    2.5 Demand Response Performance Adjustment
    2.6 Determination of Undeployed Availability
        2.6.1 Dispatchable Demand Response Resources
        2.6.2 Block Demand Response Resources
        2.6.3 Conservative Operations Demand Response Programs
        2.6.4 Emergency Demand Response Programs
    2.7 Newly Accredited Demand Response Resource and RRDRP
3   Behind-The-Meter ResourceGeneration Reporting and Documentation
4   Non-Dispatchable or Non-Controllable Registered Demand Response Programs and
    Non-Controllable and Non-Dispatchable Demand Response Programs/Behind-The-
    Meter GenerationResources


       1. DEFINITIONS

Accredited Capacity – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

As-Committed Maximum Economic Capacity Operating Limit – The Maximum Economic
Capacity Operating Limit at the time the commitment or deployment instruction effective during
the interval was issued.

Authorized Outage – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Average Deployment – Calculated for each hourly interval by averaging the Deployment during
each 5-minute interval within the hour or zero when there is not a Deployment in a 5-minute
interval.

Baseline – For Demand Response Resources using the calculated Resource production option
described in 4.1.2.1 (1) (b) of Attachment AE to the Tariff, the Baseline is the submitted hourly
baseline described in 4.1.2.1 (3) of Attachment AE to the Tariff associated with the Demand
 Response Resource. If a baseline is not submitted, the Baseline will equal the Net Generating
Capability plus the Firm Service Level. For Demand Response Resources using the submitted
Resource production option, the Baseline is equal to the Metered Load plus the Demand Response
Resource output used in settlements described in 4.1.2.1 (1) (a) of Attachment AE to the Tariff.

Block Demand Response Resource – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Commitment Status – As defined in the Integrated Marketplace Protocols.

Conservative Operations Demand Response Program – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Deliverable Capacity – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Demand Response Capacity – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Demand Response Performance Adjustment – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Demand Response Resource – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Deployment – The Real-Time Megawatt load reduction instruction issued to a Block Demand
Response Resource or a Reliability Registered Demand Response Program by SPP’s control
system for an interval. For Block Demand Response Resources, the Deployment includes the
instruction for Energy and Contingency Reserve products defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Dispatchable Demand Response Resource – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Dispatch Status – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Emergency Demand Response Program – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Firm Capacity – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Firm Service Level – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Load Responsible Entity (“LRE”) – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Maximum Availability – Defined below in each section 2.5 of this Business Practice.

Maximum Daily Energy – As defined in the Integrated Marketplace Protocols.

Maximum Daily Starts – As defined in the Integrated Marketplace Protocols.

Maximum Run Time – As defined in the Integrated Marketplace Protocols.
 Maximum Weekly Starts – As defined in the Integrated Marketplace Protocols.

Maximum Economic Capacity Operating Limit – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Maximum Emergency Capacity Operating Limit – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Metered Load – For Dispatchable Demand Response Resources and Block Demand Response
Resources, Metered Load is the 5-minute billable meter determinant defined in the Integrated
Marketplace Protocols section 4.5.9.1. For Conservative Operations Demand Response Programs
and Emergency Demand Response Programs, Metered Load is the hourly load value submitted to
SPP by the respective metering agent.

Minimum Economic Capacity Operating Limit – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Minimum Run Time – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Net Generating Capability – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Operating Tolerance – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Peak Demand – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Pre-Season Requirement – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Reliability Registered Demand Response Program – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Resource – As defined in Part I, Section 1 of the Tariff.

Resource Adequacy Requirement – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

RTBM Effective Control Mode – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Setpoint Instruction - As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Summer Season – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Undeployed Availability – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.

Variable Energy Resource – As defined in Attachment AE of the Tariff.

Winter Season – As defined in Attachment AA of the Tariff.
        2. DEMAND RESPONSE RESOURCES AND RRDRPS

As shown in the diagram below, two categories of registered demand response are outlined in
Attachment AA of the SPP OATT for LREs to qualify in meeting their Pre-Season Requirement
and Resource Adequacy Requirement: Demand Response Resources and Reliability Registered
Demand Response Programs. The registration in the SPP Integrated Marketplace for each resource
type will determine how the resource is accredited and qualified for the upcoming applicable
seasons. For purposes of Attachment AA, the two different types of Demand Resource Resources
will be accredited the same and have the same resource adequacy qualification requirements. As
for the two separate Reliability Registered Demand Response Programs, the two different
categories will be accredited differently and have separate resource adequacy requirements based
on expectation of availability and deployment. Non-Registered Demand Response Programs shall
be considered in the LRE’s Peak Demand in accordance with Attachment AA of the SPP OATT.

Behind-The-Meter Generation shall not be qualified as Demand Response Resource or RRDRP
in accordance with Attachment AA of the SPP OATT as such resources represent load curtailment
programs. Behind-The-Meter Generation can be qualified as Firm Capacity or Deliverable
Capacity as outlined in Attachment AA.




              2.1. IDENTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS

All Demand Response Resource and RRDRPs C will be qualified as Demand Response Capacity,
which will not be considered a reduction to Peak Demand, for purposes of Attachment AA.
 The size of the resource shall be the aggregation of all load delivery points for which the Demand
Response Resource or RRDRP is associated with. The documentation requirements in this
Business Practice state that entities identify the delivery points or meter locations associated with
each resource.

The aggregated, simultaneous impact of all loads associated with an individual resource shall be
used in determining the Demand Response Resource’s or RRDRP’s Net Generating Capability,
Firm Service Level, and other data variables used for calculating the resource’s Demand Response
Performance Adjustment. If one meter location or discrete point of delivery is associated with
more than one Demand Response Resource or RRDRP, then the LRE or Market Participant shall
register the metered loads separately or identify on a more granular metering level which points
are associated with each respective resource.

              2.2. PROGRAM IDENTIFICATION TIMELINE

Each LRE is responsible for identifying how a Demand Response Resource or RRDRP shall be
qualified for the upcoming applicable season. If an LRE does not identify qualification changes to
existing resources, the Transmission Provider will apply the previous applicable season’s
registration designation for determining the resource’s Demand Response Performance
Adjustment. The determination of Accredited Capacity for new resources that do not meet the
identification deadline would follow the procedures for new Demand Response Resources and
RRDRPs. The diagram below shows the timeline of resource identification and accreditation
determination.
               2.3. DEMAND RESPONSE REPORTING AND DOCUMENTATION

Documentation of a Demand Response Resource or RRDRP shall meet the following requirements
to qualify resources in accordance with Attachment AA of the SPP Tariff:

   1. Demand Response Resource and RRDRPs must be identified to the Transmission Provider
      through the Workbook.
   2. The Firm Service Level and Net Generating Capability must be submitted for the upcoming
      applicable season to the Transmission Provider through the Workbook.
   3. Identification of the load delivery points associated with each Demand Response Resource
      and RRDRP.
   4. Each LRE must provide documentation to the Transmission Provider with the size (MW)
      and type of Demand Response Resource or RRDRP.
   5. Testing documentation shall include the time and date of testing, the type of Demand
      Response Resource or RRDRP, the highest level of projected deployment achieved, the
      LRE load at the time of deployment and the amount of deployment achieved, and any other
      information needed to verify program testing requirements are met.
   6. An authorized representative of the LRE must sign the documentation.


              2.4. EMERGENCY DEMAND RESPONSE LIMIT

The Emergency Demand Response Limit (“Emergency DR Limit”) shall be based on the historical
real-time supply that exceeds the real-time demand, which for the purpose of this description will
be called Real-Time Remaining Capacity (“RTRC”). The real-time supply shall be the total offered
economic maximums for all non-Variable Energy Resources registered in the Integrated
Marketplace, plus the actual dispatch MWs for Variable Energy Resources for the applicable SPP
Balancing Authority Area. The real-time demand shall be based on the load being served in the
applicable SPP Balancing Authority Area. No real-time net import or export shall be considered
when determining the RTRC. The RTRC shall be calculated using approved Real-Time Balancing
Market studies for up to the past four (4) years. The RTSC calculation shall only consider intervals
during the Summer Season and Winter Season. To determine the limit, all RTRC values will be
sorted from highest to lowest and assigned a percentile-based occurrence within the data set. The
Emergency DR Limit shall be the applicable SPP Balancing Authority Area risk tolerance of
entering an EEA1 to access this capacity of 2-3 days of occurrence during the Summer Season and
Winter Season. The Emergency DR Limit is established in the SPP Planning Criteria and shall be
applied to both the Summer Season and Winter Season.

The Emergency DR Limit shall be allocated to LREs that notify the Transmission Provider they
plan to qualify Emergency Demand Response Programs for the upcoming applicable season by
the deadlines outlined in Attachment AA of the SPP OATT.in Attachment AA of the SPP
 Only LREs that identify or have carry over identification from the previous applicable season will
be included in the allocation of the Emergency DR Limit. In order to determine the amount each
applicable LRE receives, each LRE’s forecasted Peak Demand for the upcoming applicable season
will be compared to the total forecasted Peak Demand from all LREs considered to receive a
portion of the Emergency DR Limit. The forecasted Peak Demand from the most recent Workbook
submission will be used for the analysis. The example below shows how the Emergency DR Limit
is allocated between 6 LREs that plan on qualifying Emergency Demand Response Programs for
the upcoming season. The total Accredited Capacity from all Emergency Demand Response
Programs for each LRE cannot exceed the specific LRE’s allocated portion of the Emergency DR
Limit for the upcoming applicable season.

Assumptions:

    Total Peak Demand of 6 LREs: 13,710 MW

    Emergency DR Limit for the applicable SPP Balancing Authority Area: 3,500 MW

    Emergency DR allocation ratio: 3,500 MW / 13,710 MW = 25.53%

            LRE             FORECASTED             EMERGENCY           ALLOCATION OF
                          SUMMER SEASON                DR               EMERGENCY DR
                           PEAK DEMAND             ALLOCATION          LIMIT (MW) [C] =
                              (MW) [A]              RATIO [B]              [A] * [B]


    A                   1,200                     25.53%             306.3


    B                   1,400                     25.53%             357.4


    C                   3,000                     25.53%             765.9


    D                   6,000                     25.53%             1,531.7


    E                   2,000                     25.53%             510.6


    F                   110                       25.53%             28.1


    Total               13,710                                       3,500
               2.5. DEMAND RESPONSE PERFORMANCE ADJUSTMENT

As outlined in Attachment AA of the SPP OATT, the Accredited Capacity for Demand Response
Resource and RRDRPs is determined using the program’s Net Generating Capability and Demand
Response Performance Adjustment. The Demand Response Performance Adjustment will be a
percentage value determined by the formula as follows.

𝐷𝑒𝑚𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒 𝑃𝑒𝑟𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒 𝐴𝑑𝑗𝑢𝑠𝑡𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡
  (actual metered load − Firm Service Level − Undeployed Availability − Authorized Outage)
=                                                                                          𝑥 100%
                                  Net Generating Capability



The Demand Response Performance Adjustment shall be calculated on an interval basis. Demand
Response Resource calculations will be on a 5-minute granularity while RRDRPs will be on an
hourly granularity. Then, all applicable intervals for evaluation applied to the resource type will
be averaged together for the applicable season and year. The figure below is an example of how
the Demand Response Performance Adjustment for each interval is determined.




The most recent 3 years of historical data will be used when determining the Demand Response
Performance Adjustment for Demand Response Resource and RRDRPs, beginning with 2026
Summer Season. The Demand Response Performance Adjustment shall be 0% for years prior to
2026, similar to the application of new Demand Response Resource and RRDRPs, to account for
the transition and integration of the demand response policy. As more data becomes available, it
 will be integrated year over year until the 0% Demand Response Performance Adjustment
application fully rolls off by 2030.

The average performance across the applicable interval will be considered. For example, the
metered load for a RRDRP might be volatile within a given hour ranging from 10 MW to 20 MW.
But the average metered load in the hour results in 12 MW. Therefore, the 12 MW will be
considered in the calculation of the Demand Response Performance Adjustment, which considers
intra-hour partial deployment for a resource’s performance. The example below shows the partial
accreditation applied for an RRDRP.




              2.6. DETERMINATION OF UNDEPLOYED AVAILABILITY

Below are the sections listing how Undelployed Availability will be determined for each resource
type. Undeployed Availability shall only be considered on intervals when the resource is not
instructed to fully deploy.

                    2.6.1.   DISPATCHABLE DEMAND RESPONSE RESOURCES

For determining the Undeployed Availability of a Dispatchable Demand Response Resource in a
Real-Time 5-minute interval, the criteria below apply.
 In these criteria for Dispatchable Demand Response Resources, the Maximum Availability in a
Real-Time 5-minute interval is equal to the greater of (1) zero, and (2) the lesser of (i) the Metered
Load minus the Firm Service Level or (ii) the Net Generating Capability minus the Firm Service
Level.

       1. If the Metered Load is less than or equal to the Firm Service Level, then the Undeployed
          Availability will be zero.

       2. If all the criteria below are true, then the Undeployed Availability will be equal to the
          lesser of (1) the Maximum Emergency Capacity Operating Limit, or (2) the Maximum
          Availability for that interval.

               a. The Metered Load is greater than the Firm Service Level.

               b. The Resource is not committed for the interval.

               c. The Commitment Status is “Market” or “Reliability” for the interval.

               d. The Resource does not have an active outage in the outage scheduler tool for
                  the interval.

               e. The Maximum Daily Starts and Maximum Weekly Starts parameters would not
                  be violated by committing the Resource in the interval.

               f. The Maximum Daily Energy, in conjunction with the Minimum Run Time and
                  Minimum Economic Capacity Operating Limit, would not be violated by
                  committing the Resource in the interval.

               g. The Maximum Run Time parameter would not be violated by committing or
                  extending the commitment of the Resource in this interval.

               h. The Dispatch Status for the Energy product is “Market” for the interval.

       3. If all the criteria below are true, then the Undeployed Availability will be the lesser of
          (1) the greater of (i) zero, and (ii) the Maximum Emergency Capacity Operating Limit
          minus the difference of (a) the Baseline and (b) the Metered Load, or (2) the Maximum
          Availability for the interval.

               a. The Metered Load is greater than the Firm Service Level.
                b. The Resource is committed and the RTBM Effective Control Mode is 1, 2, or
                  3 in the interval.

               c. If the Resource is using the calculated Resource production option described in
                  4.1.2.1 of Attachment AE to the Tariff, then the difference of the (1) Metered
                  Load, and (2) the Operating Tolerance is less than or equal to the greater of (1)
                  zero, and (2) the difference of the (i) Baseline, and the (ii) average Setpoint
                  Instruction.

               d. If the Resource is using the submitted resource production option described in
                  4.1.2.1 of Attachment AE to the Tariff, then the difference of the (1) average
                  Setpoint Instruction, and (2) the Operating Tolerance is less than or equal to the
                  submitted response.

               e. The Dispatch Status for the Energy product is “Market” for the interval.

       4. Otherwise, the Undeployed Availability will be zero for the interval.

                     2.6.2.    BLOCK DEMAND RESPONSE RESOURCES

For determining the Undeployed Availability of a Block Demand Response Resource in a Real-
Time 5-minute interval, the criteria below apply.

In these criteria for Block Demand Response Resources, the Maximum Availability in a Real-
Time 5-minute interval is equal to the greater of (1) zero, and (2) the lesser of (i) the Metered Load
minus the Firm Service Level or (ii) the Net Generating Capability minus the Firm Service Level.

       1. If the Metered Load is less than or equal to the Firm Service Level, then the Undeployed
          Availability will be equal to zero.

       2. If all the criteria below are true for the Resource, then the Undeployed Availability will
          be equal to the lesser of (1) the Maximum Economic Capacity Operating Limit, or (2)
          the Maximum Availability for that interval.

               a. The Metered Load is greater than the Firm Service Level.

               b. The Resource is not committed for the interval.

               c. The Commitment Status is “Market” or “Reliability” for the interval.
        d. There is no outage in the outage management system effective in the interval
          for the Resource.

       e. The Maximum Daily Starts and Maximum Weekly Starts parameters would not
          be violated by committing the Resource in the interval.

       f. The Maximum Daily Energy, in conjunction with Minimum Run Time and
          Minimum Economic Capacity Operating Limit, would not be violated by
          committing the resource in the interval.

       g. The Maximum Run Time parameter would not be violated by committing or
          extending the commitment of the Resource in this interval.

       h. The Dispatch Status for the Energy product is “Market” for the interval.

3. If all the criteria below are true, then the Undeployed Availability will be the lesser of
   (1) the greater of (i) zero, and (ii) the As-Committed Maximum Economic Capacity
   Operating Limit minus the difference of (a) the Baseline and (b) the Metered Load, or
   (2) the Maximum Availability for the interval.

       a. The Metered Load is greater than the Firm Service Level.

       b. The Resource is committed and the RTBM Effective Control Mode is 1, 2 or 3
          in the interval.

       c. If the Resource is using the Calculated Resource Production Option, then the
          difference of the (1) Metered Load, and (2) the Operating Tolerance is less than
          or equal to the greater of (1) zero, and (2) the difference of the (i) Baseline, and
          the (ii) Deployment.

       d. If the Resource is using the Submitted Resource Production Option, then the
          difference of the (1) Deployment, and (2) the Operating Tolerance is less than
          or equal to the submitted response.

       e. The Dispatch Status for the Energy product is “Market” for the interval.

4. Otherwise, the Undeployed Availability will be zero for the interval.

For determining the Undeployed Availability of a Conservative Operations Demand Response

               a. The Metered Load is greater than the Firm Service Level.

 1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 PURPOSE

This Business Practice outlines the procedure the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) shall use to
perform the Post Season Analysis as required in Section 12 of Attachment AA. Additionally, the
Business Practice outlines the normalization of actual and forecasted peak load data, which is
necessary to complete the Post-Season Analysis.

2. PRE-SEASON AND POST SEASON ANALYSIS

Pre-Season Analysis
A pre-season analysis, described in Attachment AA Section 5, will be performed to determine
whether the LRE has demonstrated sufficient capacity to meet the Pre-Season Requirement.
The Pre-Season Requirement utilizes the LRE’s forecasted Net Peak Demand, also known as the
Pre-Season Net Peak Demand. The LRE will submit qualified capacity to meet the Pre-Season
Requirement, which will also be used when evaluating the post-season Resource Adequacy
Requirement. The Pre-Season Requirement is represented in the equation below:


   Pre-Season Requirement = Pre-Season Net Peak Demand +
                              Pre-Season Net Peak Demand * ACAP PRM


Post Season Analysis
A post season analysis will be performed after the season just completed (summer or winter as
applicable) to compare each Load Responsible Entity’s (LRE’s) actual seasonal Net Peak
Demand to the LRE’s forecasted peak demand. The LRE’s forecasted peak demand, also
referred to in Attachment AA and this Business Practice as the Pre-Season Net Peak Demand,
which is intended to be the peak load net the impact of weather as accounted for in the weather
normalization outlined in this Business Practice, will be obtained from the Resource Adequacy
Workbook submissions for the applicable season and compared to the LRE’s actual peak
demand. Actual peak demand records will be sourced from the Integrated Marketplace
settlement system. The analysis is intended to evaluate each LRE’s planning forecast
consistency and can be used to develop improvements to the resource adequacy process. The
difference of the forecast and actuals will then be adjusted for registered Demand Response
Resources and RRDRPs that were deployed during the hour of the LRE’s actual Peak Demand
(as discussed in Section 4 of this Business Practice), and further adjusted by a weather
normalization process based on the LRE’s forecast methodology or using the default Staff
forecast regression equations (as described in Section 5 and Section 6 of this BPM).
The final peak demand, once adjusted for registered deployment, weather normalization, and
certain Firm Power arrangements, is referred to as the Post Season Net Peak Demand in
Attachment AA and this Business Practice. The final Summer Season Resource Adequacy
Requirement and Winter Season Resource Adequacy Requirement will be calculated using the
 Post Season Net Peak Demand of the LRE for the Summer Season and the Post Season Net Peak
Demand of the LRE for the season. The Resource Adequacy Requirement is represented by the
equation below:


   Resource Adequacy Requirement = Post Season Net Peak Demand +
                                    Post Season Net Peak Demand * ACAP PRM


Resource Adequacy Requirement Compliance
Compliance with the Resource Adequacy Requirement will be determined by comparing the
LRE qualified capacity submitted for the Pre-Season Requirement with the final Resource
Adequacy Requirement as outlined in Attachment AA of the SPP OATT. An error allowance
shall be applied to the Post-Season Net Peak Demand, and will consider the weather
normalization process based on the following:

   (a) LREs with Post-Season Net Peak Demand values of at least 500MW, prior to the
       adjustment to reflect the contract amount of Firm Power with another entity as specified
       in Attachment AA Section 8.2 of the SPP OATT, shall have their Post-Season Net Peak
       Demand adjusted down 3% prior to the adjustment to reflect the contract amount of Firm
       Power with another entity as specified in Attachment AA Section 8.2 of the SPP OATT;

   (b) LREs with Post-Season Net Peak Demand values above 10MW but less than 500MW,
       prior to the adjustment to reflect the contract amount of Firm Power with another entity
       as specified in Attachment AA Section 8.2 of the SPP OATT, shall have their Post-
       Season Net Peak Demand adjusted down 2% plus an additional 5MW subtracted prior to
       the adjustment to reflect the contract amount of Firm Power with another entity as
       specified in Attachment AA Section 8.2 of the SPP OATT;

   (c) LREs with Post-Season Net Peak Demand values less than or equal to 10MW, prior to
       the adjustment to reflect the contract amount of Firm Power with another entity as
       specified in Attachment AA Section 8.2 of the SPP OATT, shall have their Post-Season
       Net Peak Demand adjusted down 50% prior to the adjustment to reflect the contract
       amount of Firm Power with another entity as specified in Attachment AA Section 8.2 of
       the SPP OATT;

In the event the LRE’s adjusted Post-Season Net Peak Demand is less than zero, the LRE’s Post-
Season Net Peak Demand shall be set to zero.

 3.     WEATHER NORMALIZATION METHODOLOGY

Weather normalization enables consistent and fair assessment of load forecast accuracy and
resource adequacy compliance by removing weather-driven variability. Weather normalization
processes to calculate the Post Season Net Peak Demand will employ a regression-based
methodology, which is the predominant approach in the industry. This approach balances
interpretability and accuracy, allowing for the differentiation of peak load driven by weather
versus other non-weather factors. This method will ensure that the forecast error is appropriately
attributed to weather versus non-weather drivers, providing clearer insights into forecast risk.

Methodologies should address concerns regarding historical forecast to actual variances, which
might otherwise attribute missed forecast to other factors. By systematically normalizing for
weather, LRE performance will be based on ability to provide accurate forecasts under normal
weather conditions.

Weather normalization processes will generally involve adjusting historical loads based on the
difference between actual weather variables and their long-term normal values. This adjustment
will quantify the changes in load that would have occurred had normal conditions been present,
using coefficients derived from forecasting models.

4.     DETERMINATION OF ACTUAL PEAK DEMAND

After the completion of the season, the submitted metered hourly load data on the final
Scheduled Settlement Statement will be requested from the Settlements Department for all
market settlement load delivery points. The final Scheduled Settlement Statement shall be
defined as the actual metered load used for an S120 Scheduled Settlement Statement for
purposes of this Business Practice 8600.The load delivery points will be mapped and aggregated
into LRE values equivalent to the LRE’s load points considered in its Pre-Season Peak Demand.

The Transmission Provider will determine the actual Peak Demand and peak hour for each LRE.
For LREs that have Behind-The-Meter Generation not registered in the SPP Integrated
Marketplace, Demand Response Resources, or RRDRPs, the Transmission Provider will consider
the impact of each Behind-The-Meter Generation, Demand Response Resource, or RRDRP to
determine the sole LRE peak hour to be used in the LRE’s Post-Season Net Peak Demand in
accordance with Attachment AA. Actual Behind-The-Meter Generation hourly output for
resources not registered in the SPP Integrated Marketplace shall be provided to the Transmission
Provider no later than sixty (60) Calendar Days after the conclusion of the applicable season. In
the event that the actual Behind-The-Meter Generation data is not timely provided to the
Transmission Provider, the entire Accredited Capacity amount will be added to the hourly load
data when determining the actual Peak Demand.
 Transmission losses will be added back to the actual hourly load data to be consistent with the
requirements for the forecasted Peak Demand submissions. The delivery loss factor or application
assumptions listed in Schedule M of the SPP Tariff shall be applied to the LRE’s actual Peak
Demand for the zone corresponding to the location of the LRE’s load.

4.1 TREATMENT OF WAPA AND LRE CO-SUPPLIED LOADS

This section is applicable to LREs that have contractual allocations from Western Area Power
Administration (WAPA), and portions of their load is served and reported by WAPA within a
WAPA Transmission Zone using the Co-Supply methodology. For these LREs, the Pre-Season
Peak Demand should account for both the LRE co-supplied supplied load forecast and the
WAPA load forecast, ensuring consideration of the load that is intended to be served by
WAPA. For these LREs, the Post-Season Peak Demand should include the LRE co-supplied
load and the WAPA supplied load at the time of the total load (LRE+WAPA) peak hour. The
contracted capacity of internal Firm Power agreements shall be considered in determining the
LRE’s Pre-Season Net Peak Demand and Post Season Net Peak Demand in accordance with
Attachment AA.

4.2 TREATMENT OF STATION SERVICE LOADS

Station service or auxiliary loads (such as fan motors, pump motors, and other equipment) of
generating resources that are essential to the operation of a generating resource are not required
to be included in the Pre-Season Peak Demand or Post Season Peak Demand unless serving as
retail load at the time of peak.

4.3 IMPACTS OF EMERGENCY TIES

For LREs that have loads that are normally located in external Balancing Authority Areas and
are only located in the SPP Balancing Authority Area(s) during emergency switching events, an
evaluation of those emergency switching events will take place after the season. For LREs that
are determined to have set a seasonal peak due to use of “Emergency Ties”, and it can be
determined that the load that had switched over to the SPP Balancing Authority Area(s) during
that event was forecasted to be in an external Balancing Authority Area, the impacts of that load
will be removed from the Post Season Net Peak Demand.

PEAK DEMAND

After the metered Net Peak Demand has been adjusted for registered Demand Response
Resource and RRDRP deployment, all relevant weather data for the applicable weather stations
used by the LRE will be obtained from the public sources identified by the LRE. Hourly load
data for the LRE will be matched up for the appropriate hourly weather data for the weather
stations identified by the LRE. When the LRE peak hour has been identified, the appropriate
weather data will be identified and entered into the regression equation provided by the LRE in
the workbook submittals.

       Where

               α0 = 1468

               α1 = -28.88

               α2 = 0.26

It is then determined at the peak hour, the temperature at the LRE weather station was 93 degrees
F with 55% relative humidity.

The Temperature-Humidity Index (THI) is determined to be

       Temperature-Humidity Index (THI)= 93 + 0.55 * (0.55-0.4) * max (93-58,0) = 95.9

       Temperature-Humidity Index squired (THI^2) = 9,194

The weather normalized load is determined to be

       Load = 1468 + (-28.88*95.9) + (0.26 *9,194) = 1,089MW

The weather normalized load value above is considered in the adjustment of the LRE’s actual
Net Peak Demand.

Method for Application of the Adjustment

The method for applying the adjustment is further described below.

The 1,089MW value above would be compared to the LRE’s pre-season forecast that assumes
normal weather. Then, depending upon whether the weather was normal, warmer than normal,
or cooler than normal, the adjusted metered LRE peaks are further adjusted for the weather.

There are two examples listed below.

Example 1) Assume the LRE provided a Pre-Season Net Peak Demand forecast of 1,000MW
and had an adjusted metered Net Peak Demand of 1,300MW. The adjusted metered Net Peak
Demand is then adjusted to take into account the weather normalization adjustment (1,089MW –
1,000MW= 89MW) for 1,211MW (1,300MW – 89MW). This value then has the 3% tolerance
applied (1,211 * (1- 0.03) = 1,174MW). The capacity provided by the LRE would then be
compared to the RAR of a net peak demand of 1,174MW.
 Example 2) Assume the LRE provided a Pre-Season Net Peak Demand forecast of 1,100MW
and the LRE had an adjusted metered Net Peak Demand of 1,189MW. The adjusted metered Net
Peak Demand is greater than the weather adjusted Net Peak Demand by 100MW. In this
instance no adjustment for weather is needed for the adjusted metered Net Peak Demand. The
3% tolerance is then applied to the adjusted metered Post Season Net Peak Demand of
1,189MW, which leaves a final adjustment to the Post Season Net Peak Demand of 1,153MW
(1,189 * (1 – 0.03)). The capacity provided by the LRE at the beginning of the season would
then be compared to the RAR of a net peak demand of 1,153MW.

A.1.1TEMPERATURE

  Hourly Temperature: Direct hourly temperature observations (e.g., in Fahrenheit) from
  selected weather stations are fundamental as they directly correlate with heating and cooling
  demands. Electricity consumption is highly responsive to temperature, with heating demand
  rising during cold winters and cooling demand increasing during hot summers. The use of
  electric heating systems, air conditioners, and other temperature-dependent appliances leads
  to marked variations in energy usage depending on seasonal conditions. However, these
  weather-driven fluctuations can make it difficult to assess the underlying trends in energy
  consumption. For instance, a mild winter may lead to lower energy usage than normal, while
  an unusually hot summer may drive higher-than-expected demand for cooling, which can
  create challenges in grid management and forecasting.

  Temperature values should be obtained from selected NOAA Integrated Surface Database
  (ISD) weather. If more than one weather station data is used for the zone, the average of the
  temperatures will be utilized as the average temperature of the zone. This average will be
  modeled as an hourly factor for all weather years being modeled.
   Moving Average Temperatures: To capture the cumulative effect of temperature on load,
  moving averages of past hourly temperatures will be included. These can range from a few
  hours (e.g., MA_3 for the current hour and previous two hours) up to several days (e.g.,
  MA_72 for the previous three days). Research indicates that moving averages, particularly
  MA_3, can be more significant in determining daily peak hourly load than just the coldest
  daily temperature. For summer peaks, moving averages of past temperatures tend to be
  higher or similar to the peak hour temperature, reflecting sustained heat impacts. For winter
  peaks, past hours are typically as cold or colder than the peak hour temperature, indicating
  sustained cold impacts.

A.1.2 COOLING DEGREE DAYS (CDD) AND HEATING DEGREE DAYS (HDD)

  Annual Aggregation: CDD and HDD (e.g., base 65°F) aggregated to annual data by zone
  will be used as explanatory variables in the econometric models for annual energy forecasts.
  This data is necessary for explaining variations in annual energy consumption due to heating
  and cooling demands

  Long-Term Normals: For projections and normalization, CDD and HDD values are
  typically held constant at their 30-year normal values from NOAA1314. However, an
  assessment may be undertaken to determine whether such long-term normals remain
  appropriate given recent climate shifts, potentially incorporating rolling averages or adjusting
  the look-back period.

A.1.3 HUMIDITY

  Relative Humidity: The level of humidity can affect comfort levels and thus air conditioning
  demand, even at similar temperatures. Its impact will be assessed for inclusion in the
  regression models, particularly for summer peaks.

  Temperature-Humidity Index (THI): THI combines temperature and humidity into a
  single value that better reflects the perceived heat on the human body, which drives cooling-
  related electricity demand. By factoring in the human comfort level, which is significantly
  impacted by humidity, THI can provide a more practical input for forecasting models than
  temperature or humidity alone.

A.1.4 PRECIPITATION

  Precipitation data will be considered where it significantly influences specific load segments,
  such as irrigation load in certain agricultural areas. The type of precipitation (e.g., rainfall in
  inches) and its timing (e.g., daily totals) will be relevant.

A.1.5 OTHER METEOROLOGICAL VARIABLES

  Wind Patterns: Wind speed can influence heating and cooling needs (wind chill, heat
  dissipation) and will be considered.
   Cloud Cover/Solar Radiation: For regions with significant solar generation, cloud cover
  can impact net load. Data from the National Solar Radiation Database may be integrated, and
  its influence on demand will be explored.

  Other Meteorological Variables: Humidity, wind patterns, and irradiance data (and
  conversely cloud cover) may be considered where their impact on demand can be statistically
  modeled and proven significant, particularly for distinguishing weather-sensitive load from
  other influences. Irradiance data and wind data may take longer to obtain due to reporting
  cycles of NOAA, and may not be available for use for some processes – like the Peak Demand
  Assessment.

A.1.6 NON-WEATHER VARIABLES AND ECONOMETRIC CONSIDERATIONS

  To accurately isolate weather's impact, the models provided by LREs must also account for
  non-weather drivers. For LREs that do not provide weather normalization processes, any
  projected ‘natural’ load growth anticipated should be provided along with any planned or
  known large load additions.

  Economic Factors: Macro-economic data such as personal income, gross state product
  (GSP), employment (manufacturing, non-farm), electricity prices, and natural gas prices will
  be included in the econometric models. These variables capture overall growth and economic
  activity impacting electricity consumption.

  Population: Demographic changes directly influence overall load growth.

  Energy Efficiency (EE) Programs: The impact of existing EE programs and demand
  response will be incorporated to ensure load forecasts are benchmarked to metered load
  levels that reflect these savings. Adjustments for EE programs will be made at the zonal
  level.

  New Large Loads/Technological Shifts: Significant customer additions, technological
  shifts (e.g., DER adoption, electrification, advanced HVAC systems), and behavioral changes
  can impact load patterns and will be considered to the extent data allows. The models will
  aim to distinguish weather-sensitive load from these other influences, acknowledging this can
  be complex.
